evidence.claim: Congress authorized Kinzua Dam for flood control after the destructive Pittsburgh-area flood of 1936.
evidence.quote: In 1936, a major flood struck the Pittsburgh metropolitan area and caused widespread damage. This prompted Congress to pass the Flood Control Acts of 1936 and 1938, authorizing the construction of a dam on the Allegheny River.

evidence.claim: The Army Corps of Engineers began construction in 1960 and completed the dam in 1965; filling continued until 1967.
evidence.quote: Construction of the dam was not begun by the US Army Corps of Engineers until 1960. It was completed in 1965, and the filling of the reservoir continued until 1967.

evidence.claim: Federal condemnation took Seneca land for the reservoir and forced residents to relocate.
evidence.quote: Federal condemnation of tribal lands to be flooded for the project displaced more than 600 Seneca members

evidence.claim: Begin at Route 321 and Longhouse Drive, passing Red Bridge Recreation Area before climbing toward the Old Powerhouse.
evidence.quote: The byway begins at the intersection of Route 321 and Longhouse Drive. As you begin your drive you will pass Red Bridge Recreation Area

evidence.claim: Beyond the Bradford Ranger Station, Route 59 leads past the Rimrock turnoff to the reservoir, with Kinzua Beach on the left.
evidence.quote: After the entrance for Rimrock you will reach the reservoir, with Kinzua Beach to the left and Wolf Run Marina to the right.

evidence.claim: The Old Powerhouse explains how one engine could lift oil from underground.
evidence.quote: Oil was brought to the surface using the engine in the powerhouse to drive a system of belts, wheels and rod lines.

evidence.claim: Its Cooper-Bessemer single-piston engine powered belts, wheels and rod lines; the mechanism changed horizontal motion into the vertical stroke needed at the well.
evidence.quote: The mechanical trick here is to transfer the horizontal energy of the rod line to a vertical motion that pulls the sucker rod up and down in the well.

evidence.claim: Its Cooper-Bessemer single-piston engine
evidence.quote: Cooper-Bessemer single piston, 22.5 horsepower oil field engine

evidence.claim: The scrap-metal building dates to 1939 and worked for half a century.
evidence.quote: scrap metal walls of this 1939 powerhouse that was in use for half a century.

evidence.claim: That machinery belongs to the larger history of the Bradford oil field, founded in 1875.
evidence.quote: The founding of the Bradford oil field in 1875 brought a new dimension to America's oil industry.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service and its partners restored the powerhouse as an interpretive site, preserving a place to understand the equipment and its work.
evidence.quote: with the help of many partners, the US Forest Service has restored the powerhouse as an interpretive site.

evidence.claim: Early twentieth-century oil fields used different pumping systems, each with its own solution to moving power from engine to well.
evidence.quote: Each oil field in the early 1900's had a different pumping system with its own unique solutions to the engineering problems at hand.

evidence.claim: The water beside the byway is a constructed landscape.
evidence.quote: The Allegheny Reservoir is a man-made lake created along the Allegheny River with the construction of the Kinzua Dam in 1965.

evidence.claim: Kinzua Dam was built for flood control, and the resulting reservoir extends into Pennsylvania and New York.
evidence.quote: a reservoir along the Allegheny River in Pennsylvania and New York

evidence.claim: Kinzua Dam was built for flood control
evidence.quote: The dam was authorized by the United States Congress as a flood control measure

evidence.claim: Its creation flooded Seneca land and forced people from their homes.
evidence.quote: flooded some of the lands of the Seneca Nation. The residents in these areas were forced to move.

evidence.claim: The federal government also condemned most of the Cornplanter Tract in Pennsylvania, including a cemetery containing Cornplanter’s remains and those of descendants and followers.
evidence.quote: the government also condemned most of the historic Cornplanter Tract

evidence.claim: The reservoir now lies within a landscape of national forest, state park and the Seneca Nation’s Allegany Reservation.
evidence.quote: The Allegheny Reservoir is surrounded by the Allegheny National Forest in Pennsylvania and Allegheny State Park and the Seneca Nation's Allegany Reservation in New York.

evidence.claim: Trees grow through the boulders at Jakes Rocks, and sometimes on top of them.
evidence.quote: trees growing through, and sometimes on, the large boulders.

evidence.claim: Hardened paths lead through the woods to a rock outcrop overlooking Jackson Bay, Kinzua Dam and the surrounding forest.
evidence.quote: Wander on hardened paths through the woods to the overlook. Stand on the rock outcrop to see expansive views of Jackson Bay on the Allegheny Reservoir, Kinzua Dam and the surrounding forest.

evidence.claim: The trail loops through the day-use area, passing large boulders before reaching the overlook built onto one of them.
evidence.quote: There is a trail that loops around the day use area past large boulders and to the overlook built onto a large boulder.

evidence.claim: The approach road also makes a loop, with pull-offs for views of the reservoir.
evidence.quote: The road leading up to the day use area loops around and has several scenic pull-offs where visitors can stop and view the reservoir.

evidence.claim: Wildflowers, mosses and fungi grow along the walking paths, among trees rooted through and on the rocks.
evidence.quote: As you walk try to glimpse the different wildflowers, mosses and fungus throughout the area.

evidence.claim: Mountain laurel grows along the heavily forested access road, which leads to the walking loop and its boulders.

flags: The Forest Service gives 36 miles; the material mapped length is 29.6 miles. Use the official loop description. Its driving direction reverses the strip-map mile progression; moments follow the explicit Forest Service itinerary.
No cache source explains construction or campaigning for the byway itself. Overview history covers the dam that shaped its present landscape.
Displacement history is supported only by secondary sources; a Seneca-authored source is absent. Cache alternates between 600 people and 600 families, so no displacement count is used.
Generic Forest Service alerts mention Forest Road 321, not Pennsylvania Route 321. Do not turn that banner into a byway closure.
All current claims are supported. Lake Perfidy and the song connection were omitted for focus, not lack of evidence.
